tracks.title: A key you use but never read
tracks.text: Lesson two point twelve — secrets. A deep-dive, under nexus. A key you can use… but never read. That is the whole idea, and it is stranger than it sounds. You want an agent to call Stripe, or OpenAI, or your own API. Everywhere else, that means handing the credential to the code. Here… you hand it a name. The agent works with the name. The value joins the request on the host side of the sandbox wall — after your template leaves the guest, and before the socket opens. [curious] So no instruction the agent can run — buggy, hostile, or prompt-injected — can address it. The guarantee isn't a filter. It's the absence of an API.

tracks.title: The key in the prompt
tracks.text: First — the key in the prompt. Everywhere else, calling an API means leaving the credential lying around, and there are three classic ways. First… a dot-env file the agent can read the moment it decides to. Second… an environment variable any dependency in your tree can reach. Third… a key pasted into a prompt — which is now in a context window, a transcript, and a log file… forever. [sighs] And then prompt injection turned all three from a hygiene problem into an active attack. Anyone whose text reaches your agent — a web page it reads, an email it summarizes — is partially steering a process that holds your keys. The parent nexus lesson already made the claim. Secrets stay in the engine, so there's nothing to leak. This page… is the receipts.

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: The definition. A secret is a variable the guest can name, count, and use — never read. The placeholder — secret, colon, key — is the whole of the guest-side API. The value crosses the membrane as an effect… never as data. And the design has three pieces, kept carefully apart. First… a schema layer, holding names and kinds, and no values. Second… a backend, holding the values host-side, where the guest has no reach. Third… the membrane rule — the one that makes it a guarantee instead of a hope: a secret's value crosses into the guest only as the effect of a host-brokered operation, never as a string the guest can hold. You write the name. The engine supplies the value… on its own side of the wall.

tracks.title: Marking and handling refs
tracks.text: Marking and handling refs. On the engine, a secret is just a tenant variable with one flag flipped. Picture a session. You run var set, STRIPE underscore KEY, the value, dash dash secret — and it confirms, set, secret. You run var get on it… and instead of the value you get back: secret, thirty-two bytes, ref it with the placeholder, cannot read. Length and existence — never the bytes. You run var list, and you see STRIPE underscore KEY marked secret, and brand marked plain. Then the one that teaches the whole model. You run var ref on a template that says, POST for, brand placeholder, auth, secret placeholder. And the result comes back: POST for acme — auth… and then the secret placeholder, completely intact. [curious] Read that carefully. The plain variable resolved — brand became acme. The secret did not. Its placeholder came back untouched. That is not the tool being cautious. The runtime's var ref runs in guest mode by construction — an agent calling through it physically cannot ask for the resolved value. And one more rule hides in there. A missing key stays literal too — never replaced with a blank. A broken config fails loudly at the API that rejects it… instead of succeeding quietly with an empty credential.

tracks.title: Guest mode versus host mode
tracks.text: Guest mode versus host mode. There is one branch in the resolver that is the security model. Resolution runs in one of two modes. In guest mode, vars resolve… and secrets stay literal. In host mode, everything resolves — but host mode runs only inside host-side operations, at egress, outside the guest's reach. The demo resolves one template twice. The agent writes: POST for, brand, auth, secret-token. The guest reading comes back: POST for acme, auth, and the secret placeholder still sitting there. The host reading comes back: POST for acme, auth, S-K… the real value. Same template… two readings. The agent only ever sees the first. The second exists only on the host's side of the boundary, inside the operation that opens the connection. Now follow the secret's lane through the whole trip. Picture a relay where the baton never enters the first runner's hand. Inside the sandbox, the agent builds the template with the placeholder in it, runs var ref in guest mode so the placeholder stays literal, and hands the whole template across the dock. Then — on the host side of the wall, where the guest cannot observe anything — the host injects the real value, opens the socket, and sends the request with the key. The response comes back to the host… and the host hands the agent the result. Never the key. [excited] The secret's lane never enters the sandbox at all.

tracks.title: Enforcement, not etiquette
tracks.text: Now the part that makes this physics, not etiquette. Credit where it's owed — this design borrows its schema-and-values split, and its redaction discipline, from Varlock. A genuinely good secret manager. So let's be precise about the difference, because it's the whole point. Varlock, like every careful secret manager, redacts what a process could still read. The value is in the process… and the tooling works hard to keep it from being printed, or logged, or leaked. That is real engineering. But it is a discipline — a wall of checks around bytes the process can, in principle, address. Here… the bytes are never written into the guest's memory at all. The host writes the secret into the outbound request buffer on its own side of the WebAssembly boundary — after the template leaves the sandbox, before the socket. The value is never placed into the address space the guest can reach. So no guest instruction — intended, buggy, or hostile — can point at it. [curious] There is nothing to redact… because there is nothing there. A redaction filter can have a bug. The absence of an address cannot. And this isn't asserted — it's tested at the hardest level. The sandbox security suite plants a real file on the host disk with a marker string inside, then runs guest programs in Rust, Go, C, and JavaScript that try every trick to steal it — file reads, shell spawns — and asserts that all of them fail. The secret model rides on that same wall.

tracks.title: The missing import
tracks.text: The missing import. The dock — the membrane between guest and host — exposes a fixed set of operations the guest may ask the host to perform. And the guarantee is the shape of that set. There is deliberately no secret-get. No operation that takes a name and returns a string. Adding one would defeat the whole model — and its absence is the guarantee. So here is exactly what a guest can and can't learn about a secret. First… does it exist? Yes — existence is the only secret-shaped fact a guest may observe. Second… how long is it? Yes — a byte count, from a redacted get. Third… read its value? No — there is no operation that returns it; the path does not exist. And fourth… use it in a request? Yes — by reference, the host injects it at egress, and the guest never holds it. [curious] And this pattern already ships and runs. The model-completion operation is the proof. A guest asks the host to call a language model. The host holds the OpenRouter key, reads it on its own side, makes the call — and the component never sees the key. Same rule… generalized. And because a missing name stays literal, a misconfigured secret never sends a blank credential. It fails at the API, loudly, where you can see it.

tracks.title: Use without an egress point
tracks.text: Use without an egress point. Injection-at-egress covers the common case — a credential riding in a request header. But there is a stronger move, and it's the cleanest proof that use and read are genuinely different operations. The SecretBroker lets a guest use a key… with no injection point at all. Picture a stamp on the far side of a slot. The host registers a named secret for a tenant. The only thing the guest can call is sign. The guest pushes a payload through the slot; the host presses the key against it with HMAC, and pushes back a thirty-two-byte signature. The guest gets the signature… never the key. No template, no egress, no header — the credential does real cryptographic work, and the worker never possesses it. And the broker is built for a multi-tenant world. It is tenant-scoped and revocation-aware. A revoked tenant asking to sign gets an error — revoked. A tenant reaching for another tenant's secret gets an error — unknown secret. And the tests prove the shape directly. They assert the module exports the sign operation… and no getter at all. There is no way to retrieve a secret's value, because the function that would do it was never written. [excited] This is the sharpest instance of the whole lesson — a credential doing work, with the worker that triggered it never able to see it.

tracks.title: Names in the file, values in the vault
tracks.text: Names in the file, values in the vault. So far this has been the runtime. Deployment is where you, the operator, put the real keys in — and it keeps the same split. Names are committable. Values never are. You declare the names of the secrets your engine needs in a deployment file, in plain text you can check into git — a target, an app name, and a line that says deploy-secrets: OpenRouter key, Stripe key. The values go nowhere near that file. You stage them separately. Run deploy validate, and it tells you what's still missing — ok on the deployment file, then a warning: declared secrets unset, Stripe key. Run deploy secrets set on the Stripe key, and it stages it into a locked file in your home directory, applied on the next deploy. Run deploy secrets list… and you see names only — never values. Same discipline as the runtime, one layer out. And the two checks differ on purpose. Validate warns on a missing secret. But apply hard-fails — it will not deploy an engine missing a credential it declared it needs. Now picture the round-trip. Names come from the org file — the one you commit. Values come from a file locked to owner-only — the one that stays on your machine. They converge only at apply, which spawns the provider recipe in a clean environment and hands the keys to its secrets hook. And two dotted lines are the load-bearing part: neither the names nor the values are ever baked into the image. The runtime image is byte-identical for everyone who runs it — the secrets arrive at deploy time, through the provider, and live in the provider's own store.

tracks.title: Delivery hooks
tracks.text: Delivery hooks. The spawn is deliberate about not leaking. The kit invokes the provider recipe in a clean environment — starting from nothing, passing each secret as an explicit key-equals-value argument, plus a list of every name in play. The staged secrets reach the hook without ever touching the deploying process's own environment. From there, each target delivers them its own way. First… fly — it runs fly secrets set, staged, released by the deploy that follows; the whole hook is three lines. Second… docker and podman — delivered as an env-file, the container's environment at run time, never baked into the image. Third… krunvm — and this is the honest gap; it can't carry the secrets env yet, so it tells you to use docker, podman, or a cloud provider, out loud, rather than failing in some confusing way. And fourth… your own platform — write a five-hook recipe, and secrets get their own hook; a behaviour seam, not a fork. The verdict across all of them: every shipped path delivers secrets as the workload's environment at run time… never baked into the artifact. And one secret the kit manages itself — the public bearer token. On your first cloud apply, the kit generates a two-hundred-fifty-six-bit token from a secure random source, persists it, and then never rotates it — because rotating a live token would lock out every client already talking to your engine.

tracks.title: What this isn't
tracks.text: What this isn't. The model is strong enough that it's easy to oversell, so — four honest edges. First… the host holds plaintext. Somewhere on your engine, the values sit in cleartext — the variables database, the staged secrets file, the provider's store. This protects you from the workload — the agent, its dependencies, the text steering it. It does not protect you from someone who owns your engine box. That's a different threat, for a different layer. Second… the general fetch lane is the design's endgame, not all wired today. What ships and runs right now is injection through specific host-brokered operations — model completion is the proof — plus the broker, for signing. A guest passing a secret-templated header through a generic, arbitrary fetch is the destination, not the whole present. Third… local var ref resolves secrets. On your own machine, the local tool substitutes both — because that file is already readable on your disk; it's your trust domain. The guest-host split is enforced by the runtime's resolver, not the local tool. Different rooms. And fourth… the environment backend is the only one shipped. The backend is a clean seam — 1Password, Vault, AWS, Varlock all slot in with no core change — but today the shipped one reads from configured values and the environment. The others are a swap you can make… not a feature you flip on.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Can the agent ever print my key? No. There is no read path — no operation returns a secret's value — and the sandbox suite proves it: guest programs trying to steal a planted secret all fail. Can a secret name not exist? Then the placeholder stays literal — never a blank — and the API rejects the request. It fails loudly at auth, never silently with an empty credential. Are secrets stored in the workbook file or bundle? No. They live in the engine-side store; a bundle carries references, not values. You can send the artifact without sending a credential. How do I rotate one? Re-set it and re-stage — deploy secrets set, then push. The one exception is the public bearer token… generated once, never auto-rotated, because rotating it would lock out your live clients. And — where exactly do the bytes live? At rest, a small database on the runtime. On deploy, the locked secrets file. In production, the provider's own store. [chuckles] Never in the workbook, never in the image, never in the guest's memory.

tracks.title: Back up to the nexus
tracks.text: So that's secrets. A credential the agent can name, count, and use — and never read. The value joins the request on the host side of the wall, after the template leaves the sandbox, before the socket. And the guarantee isn't a filter you have to trust — it's an API that was deliberately never written. [curious] This page proves one line the parent lesson promised: secrets stay in the engine, so there's nothing to leak. The way back up is short — nexus is the lesson this one serves. Go read how the same sandbox wall that hides your key… also seals the disk, and grants every capability by name. Everything here is built from that one boundary.
